in_text_mentions: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a ring-enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe with adjacent dural inflammation (Figure 1). The abscess was surgically drained and she was treated with intravenous meropenem (135 mg/kg/day). Her condition improved rapidly, and she had a normal mental status by Day 2. One and a half years after discharge, she has had no neurological sequelae including convulsions, and no abnormal EEG findings have been observed.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Contrast-enhanced CT panel shows a ring-enhancing hypodense brain lesion with perilesional edema and midline shift, consistent with brain abscess. b: FLAIR MRI shows a lesion with a hypointense rim and surrounding hyperintense edema, characteristic of a brain abscess capsule and vasogenic edema. c: DWI MRI demonstrates marked hyperintensity within the abscess cavity, supporting central restricted diffusion. d: ADC map shows corresponding hypointensity in the lesion, confirming restricted diffusion typical of brain abscess.

panels.figure_caption: Brain abscess detected by contrast-enhanced computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. (a) Contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan showing a low-density area with ring enhancement. (b) T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery image showing a hyperintense lesion surrounded by a thin hypointense ring. Hyperintense edema is noted. (c) Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance image demonstrating a hyperintense signal within the lesion. (d) Apparent diffusion coefficient map shows hypo-intensity within the lesion, confirming the presence of restricted diffusion.
in_text_mentions: Contrast-enhanced computerized tomography revealed a ring-enhanced lesion (15 mm × 10 mm) with perilesional edema on the posterior limb of internal capsule in the left cerebral hemisphere, with a midline shift (Figure 1(a)). Magnetic resonance imaging also demonstrated a ring-enhancing lesion (15 mm × 10 mm) with a large amount of adjacent edema and mass effect (T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery; Figure 1(b)). Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging revealed a markedly hyperintense lesion with a low apparent diffusion coefficient (Figures 1(c) and 1(d)).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Preoperative axial T1-weighted MRI shows a right frontal lesion with surrounding edema in a patient with confirmed brain abscess. B: Post-contrast T1-weighted MRI demonstrates the classic ring-enhancing right frontal brain abscess. C: Diffusion-weighted MRI shows central restricted diffusion corresponding to the abscess cavity. D: Axial T2-weighted MRI shows the right frontal abscess with perilesional edema and a hypointense capsule rim. E: Axial FLAIR MRI demonstrates hyperintense signal around the right frontal abscess consistent with vasogenic edema. F: ADC map shows low signal in the abscess core, confirming restricted diffusion.

panels.figure_caption: A 53-year-old man with reported seizures was evaluated. (A) Head CT without contrast medium reveals a round left occipital mass lesion (arrow) with hyperdense margins and a hypodense center. (B) A T-2-weighted head MRI image without contrast shows a mass (arrow) with high central signal intensity, a ring of heterogeneous peripheral signal intensity similar to that of the brain parenchyma, and a surrounding area of bright signal in the white-matter tracts. (C) On the contrast-enhanced T-1-weighted head MRI image, the mass has low signal intensity centrally that suggests the presence of fluid, and is surrounded by an enhancement ring, beyond which extends an area of low signal that indicates edema.

in_text_mentions: A plain CT scan of the head (Figure 1) revealed a left intra-axial frontal lobe lesion measuring 1.7 x 1.3 cm with surrounding edema, minimal mass effect, and no midline shift. CT scans of the abdomen, chest, and pelvis were negative for systemic malignancy.

An MRI of the brain with contrast (Figure 1) showed a peripherally enhancing left frontal intra-axial mass, in the medial posterior left frontal lobe, surrounded by vasogenic edema suspicious for neoplasm vs. abscess. There was a second punctiform area of diffusion restriction in the right frontal lobe consistent with an acute embolic infarct (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: Initial empirical therapy with piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g every 8 h) was initiated. On Day 9, neurological deterioration developed, including dysarthria, right facial droop, and generalized seizures, accompanied by fever (38.8 °C). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 47 × 31 × 43 mm lesion in the left frontal lobe with significant surrounding edema, consistent with brain abscess (Figure 1). Empirical antimicrobial coverage was broadened to vancomycin (1 g daily) and meropenem (2 g every 8 h). By Day 14, fever subsided, but neurological deficits persisted.

A computed tomography (CT) scan of his head without intravenous contrast demonstrated multiple foci of gas-containing abscesses along the margin of the craniotomy (Figure 1a). The air in the abscess was considered part of the expected post-craniotomy changes. Incision, drainage, and removal of the bone flap were promptly performed. Vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated and then narrowed to ceftriaxone and metronidazole when a Gram stain revealed many polymononuclear cells but no organisms. Despite this management, fevers continued and our patient’s

Cultures on sheep’s blood agar from the neurosurgical debridements revealed small colonies with a peripheral clearing (‘fried egg’ morphology). Through sequencing of the 16 S ribosomal subunit region at a reference laboratory, the isolate was identified as M. hominis with 100% homology to reference strains. Our patient’s antibiotics were changed to doxycycline 100mg intravenously twice per day on hospital day 24. His mental status and fevers improved significantly. The abscess had almost fully resolved by hospital day 40 (Figure 1c).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Plain CT on day 6 shows a left occipital space-occupying lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema and right lateral ventricular debris, consistent with brain abscess/ventriculitis in the reported case. B: Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI on day 6 demonstrates the classic ring-enhancing pattern of a brain abscess in the left occipital lobe. C: Diffusion-weighted imaging on day 6 shows homogeneous high signal in the left occipital lesion, representing restricted diffusion typical of a pyogenic brain abscess cavity. D: Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI on day 30 is a post-treatment follow-up showing marked interval decrease of the left occipital abscess; it still belongs to the same patient with brain abscess but is less diagnostically representative than the day-6 images.

CNS abscesses were considered the most likely diagnosis, while a neoplastic etiology was deemed unlikely (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Axial post-contrast T1 MRI shows a ring-enhancing left parietal lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema, consistent with brain abscess in the article context. B: Sagittal post-contrast T1 MRI demonstrates the ring-enhancing parietal lesion and extensive surrounding edema. C: Coronal post-contrast T1 MRI shows the ring-enhancing left parietal lesion with perilesional edema. D: DWI shows marked restricted diffusion within the lesion, a characteristic MRI feature of brain abscess. E: ADC map confirms low signal corresponding to restricted diffusion in the abscess cavity.

panels.figure_caption: Brain MRI demonstrating left parietal ring-enhancing lesion (A-C) Axial, sagittal, and coronal T1-weighted MRI obtained following IV gadolinium-based contrast administration, demonstrating an irregular ring-enhancing lesion (white arrows) in the left posterior parietal lobe measuring 4.0 x 3.0 x 2.3 cm. Associated surrounding hypointense signal is consistent with extensive vasogenic edema (white arrowheads). (D) DWI trace sequence demonstrating marked restricted diffusion (white arrow) within the lesion. (E) ADC map demonstrating a corresponding low ADC signal (white arrow), further supporting restricted diffusion.
in_text_mentions: e left posterior parietal lobe, indicating ischemic infarct versus an underlying mass lesion (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with and without IV gadolinium-based contrast revealed a 4.0 x 3.0 x 2.3 cm irregular ring-enhancing lesion with extensive perilesional edema (Figure 2). The lesion demonstrated restricted diffusion on DWI/ADC sequences, reflecting impaired movement of water molecules within the brain tissue. Given the irregular enhancement pattern and infiltrative appearance, these findings were initially interpreted as most consistent with a high-grade glioma.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (T1W, T2W, DWI). T1W: Sagittal T1-weighted MRI of a real patient with brain abscess; caption describes a low-signal lesion with annular high signal in the right parietal–temporal lobe, consistent with ring enhancement/abscess capsule. No exclusion criteria apply. T2W: Axial T2-weighted MRI shows the brain abscess with hypointense capsule, perilesional edema, and mass effect/midline shift described in the caption/in-text; direct disease attribution to brain abscess. DWI: Axial diffusion-weighted MRI shows restricted diffusion in the abscess cavity and surrounding edema/mass effect, directly attributed to brain abscess by the caption and article.

panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance images of the brain abscess. TIW = T1-weighted; T2W = T2-weighted; DWI = diffusion weighed imaging. A patchy abnormal signal was observed in the right parietal–temporal lobe, with a low signal on T1-weighted imaging surrounded by annular high signals, and a high signal on T2-weighted imaging surrounded by annular low signals around the lesion. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed high signals with patchy long T1 and long T2 signals around the lesion; the lesion appeared to be connected to the right lateral ventricle
in_text_mentions: egular shape, although brain herniation still needed to be ruled out (Fig. 1). Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed abnormal signals in the right parietal–temporal lobe, which may have been due to an abscess rupturing into the ventricle and sulcus. The presence of a tumor had yet to be excluded. There were signs of increased intracranial pressure, with compression of the right lateral ventricle and a shift in midline structures to the left. Additionally, a mass was identified in the right temporal–occipital region, accompanied by a midline shift and severe cerebral edema (Fig. 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Row A is the DWI sequence of the patient's brain MRI (with magnified ROI at right). Multiple ovoid high-signal lesions in the left MCA/PCA border zone represent the restricted diffusion of cerebral abscess (early cerebritis), a classic abscess MRI feature; the article title and caption attribute these lesions to brain abscess. B: Row B is the ADC map (with magnified ROI) showing low signal corresponding to the DWI lesions, i.e. restricted diffusion of the abscess core, a classic brain-abscess MRI signature. C: Row C is the contrast-enhanced T1 sequence (with magnified ROI) showing the patient's lesions without enhancement, consistent with the non-encapsulated early cerebritis stage of brain abscess; the panel is a supporting sequence of the same abscess lesions rather than a separate disease. D: Row D is the T2*-weighted sequence (with magnified ROI) of the same patient; the lesions show no blooming/susceptibility signal,...

Multiple lesions can be seen in the border area between the middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery in the left hemisphere. High signal intensity lesions on diffusion-weighted MRI and their corresponding low-signal lesions on the ADC, without enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI and without low signal on T2 *-weighted MRI, are seen. T2-weighted MRI shows a high signal lesion with subtle low signal in the center of the ovoid-shaped dominant peripheral lesion. Figures in the right column are magnified regions of interest from the images of the lesion marked (*).

First, the dominant left parietal lesion (see magnified view in the last column of Figure 1) has subtle low signal intensity in its center on the T2-weighted image; a low signal on T2 is often a feature of CNS infection.
